setupSteps: Learn the hinge first (no weight). Hold a broomstick, mop handle or rolled towel along your back so it touches three points: the back of the head, the upper back, and the tailbone. Hinge with a slight knee bend while keeping all three points in contact. If the tailbone leaves the stick, you are bending the spine, not hinging at the hips (Prehab Guys, Rehab Hero, snippets). Move on after about 8 clean reps (one source's rule, est.).
Choose the weight. Start with the lightest option that lets you do 10 clean slow reps with 3-4 reps left in the tank (section 7). Water bottles or a rucksack are good first loads.
Mat. A non-slip mat on a flat spot; clear 1 m x 1 m and keep the floor in front of your toes free. Put a folded towel beside you to set the weights down on.
Pick the weights up safely. Bend the knees and hips to lift them from the floor (a mini squat), keep the back flat; do not round the back to pick them up.

Grip. Hold one dumbbell in each hand with an overhand grip, palms facing the thighs, weights in front of the hips. Single-dumbbell version: hold one dumbbell upright with both hands in front of the thighs. Rucksack: hold it by the top handle or both arms against the thighs. Bottles: one in each hand.

Stance. Feet hip-width apart (sources say hip-width to about shoulder-width), toes pointing forward or slightly out, weight spread over the whole foot with a bit more towards the heels (sources vary; use the width where you feel steady).
Soft knees. Bend the knees a little, just enough to unlock them (soft knee), and keep that same bend all the way down and up. The knees do not bend further as you lower.
Stand tall and set the shoulders. Chest proud, shoulder blades gently down and back (the "back pockets" cue), ribs down, gaze about 2 m ahead on the floor so the neck stays in line with the spine.
Camera. Phone in landscape at about hip height (80-100 cm, est.), 2-2.5 m to the side (side view), full body from head to floor in frame.
Warm up 3-5 minutes (est.): march on the spot, hip circles, 5-8 bodyweight squats (Home 1), 6-8 unweighted broomstick hinges, a few glute bridges (Home 4), and one set with very light bottles.

steps.title: Stand tall holding the weights in front of the thighs
steps.action: Feet hip-width, knees softly bent, weights resting in front of the thighs, palms facing the body.
steps.feel: Weights light against the thighs, shoulders relaxed and slightly back.
steps.visualCheck: Side: ear, shoulder, hip and ankle roughly in one line; slight knee bend. Front: shoulders level, feet even, weights at the sides of the thighs.

steps.title: Brace and set the shoulders
steps.action: Lightly tighten the tummy as if about to be tapped, ribs down, shoulder blades gently down and back.
steps.feel: A firm, long trunk, not a held breath.
steps.breathing: A comfortable breath in; do not hold it for the whole rep.
steps.visualCheck: Side: ribs not flared, lower back neutral (not hollowed).

steps.title: Start the hinge: send the hips back
steps.action: Push the hips straight back, as if closing a car door behind you with your bottom. The knees stay soft and do not bend more.
steps.feel: Weight moves towards the heels; the back of the thighs begins to stretch.
steps.visualCheck: Side: hips travel backwards; shins stay nearly vertical. Front: knees stay in line with the toes.

steps.title: Slide the weights down the legs
steps.action: Let the arms hang straight and keep the weights close to the thighs and shins, as if sliding down a pole; the further the weight is from the body, the more stress on the spine (Barbell Logic, Myprotein, snippets).
steps.feel: Shoulder blades staying back; light pull in the upper back and a growing stretch in the hamstrings.
steps.visualCheck: Side: dumbbells travel close to the legs in a near-vertical line. Front: dumbbells stay beside the thighs, not out to the sides.

steps.title: Keep the back flat and the neck long
steps.action: Keep the chest proud and the spine in one long line from the tailbone to the head; look at the floor 2 m ahead, not your feet.
steps.feel: A strong long back; no pinching or rounding.
steps.breathing: Hold the comfortable breath at depth only briefly.
steps.visualCheck: Side: back flat (no hump), neck in line; no tucking of the pelvis.

steps.title: Stop at your depth
steps.action: Stop when you feel a strong stretch in the hamstrings or when the back would start to round, or when the weights reach about mid-shin, whichever comes first. Beginners often reach only knee or just below-knee height, and that is fine. Hamstring flexibility sets how low you can go; forcing more makes the back round or the knees bend (NASM, Myprotein, snippets).
steps.feel: A firm, comfortable stretch in the back of the thighs, no pain in the back.
steps.visualCheck: Side: torso tipped forward (roughly 90-120 deg at the hip, est.), knees still soft, weights at or below the knee. Front: weights close to the legs.

steps.title: Drive the hips forward to stand
steps.action: Push the feet into the floor, squeeze the bottom, and bring the hips forward under the shoulders; the back stays flat as the torso rises.
steps.feel: The bottom and back of the thighs doing the work; the weights follow the legs up.
steps.breathing: Breathe out as you stand (do not hold the breath).
steps.visualCheck: Side: hips lead the movement, torso and hips rise together; no leaning back. Front: weights close to the thighs.

steps.title: Finish tall
steps.action: Stand straight, hips under shoulders, squeeze the bottom gently; do not lean back or over-arch.
steps.feel: Tall and balanced; a calm bottom squeeze.
steps.breathing: Breathe in for the next rep.
steps.visualCheck: Side: ears over shoulders over hips; knees extended but soft (not locked back). Front: weights at the sides of the thighs.

steps.title: Set the weights down safely
steps.action: After the last rep, bend the knees and hips (a mini squat), keep the back flat, and place the weights gently on the towel or mat with a 2-3 s count.
steps.visualCheck: Side: back flat; no drop. The only sound should be a soft touch.

commonMistakes.title: Rounding the back
commonMistakes.text: Rounding the back. Why: loads the spine in a flexed position, a plausible injury mechanism named by ACE (a mechanism, not an established cause); thoracic rounding under load without strength raises risk (sources, snippets). Fix: lighter weights, stop higher up the legs, broomstick drill, film from the side.

commonMistakes.title: Bending the knees too much (squatting the movement)
commonMistakes.text: Bending the knees too much (squatting the movement). Why: shifts the work to the thighs and takes the stretch away from the hamstrings; it is one of the two most common RDL faults cited (Myprotein, snippet). Fix: soften the knees once, keep that angle, and send the hips back instead of down.

commonMistakes.title: Holding the weights away from the legs
commonMistakes.text: Holding the weights away from the legs. Why: the further the weight is from the body, the more stress on the back (Barbell Logic, snippet). Fix: slide the weights down the thighs and shins as if on a pole; keep the shoulder blades back.

commonMistakes.title: Reaching with the arms or leading with the head
commonMistakes.text: Reaching with the arms or leading with the head. Why: the movement then comes from the shoulders and upper back, not the hips. Fix: arms stay long and relaxed; hips go back first.

commonMistakes.title: Going too low for your flexibility
commonMistakes.text: Going too low for your flexibility. Why: the back rounds or the knees bend to force extra range, and extra depth adds little hamstring tension (Jeff Nippard summary, SimpliFaster, snippets). Fix: stop at the hamstring stretch, even if that is at knee height; depth comes with practice.

commonMistakes.title: Locking the knees (stiff-leg)
commonMistakes.text: Locking the knees (stiff-leg). Why: it becomes a stiff-leg deadlift, a different, more demanding exercise (snippets). Fix: keep the soft knee, no hyperextension at the top.

commonMistakes.title: Leaning back or over-arching at the top
commonMistakes.text: Leaning back or over-arching at the top. Why: loads the lower back. Fix: finish with the hips under the shoulders and a gentle bottom squeeze.

commonMistakes.title: Dropping fast and bouncing
commonMistakes.text: Dropping fast and bouncing. Why: loses control, skips the slow lowering phase, and adds noise for neighbours below. Fix: 3 s lowering count, 1 s pause, controlled stand.

commonMistakes.title: Weights too heavy too soon
commonMistakes.text: Weights too heavy too soon. Why: NASM lists weights too heavy to hold a good spinal position as a common error (snippet). Fix: use 3-4 reps in reserve; the last rep should look like the first.

commonMistakes.title: Holding the breath
commonMistakes.text: Holding the breath. Why: raises blood pressure and brings dizziness (breathing study PubMed 7741618, carried from earlier items). Fix: breathe in on the way down, out on the way up.

safetyNotes: Lower back problems: the hinge is often used in back-pain rehab, but flexed-spine hinging or going too deep can irritate it; learn the hinge unweighted, use light loads, stay flat, stop if pain increases or spreads down a leg. One source advises that people with lower back pain or hamstring injuries should avoid the single-leg version (snippet). Clinical guidance specific to the weighted dumbbell RDL: Not found.
Hamstring strain or recent hamstring pain: avoid deep stretching under load; stop at a mild stretch, not a pull. Return-to-RDL guidance: Not found.
Knee problems: the knees stay soft and almost still, so loading is mostly on the hips; use a small range, and stop with sharp pain. RDL-specific knee guidance: Not found.
Shoulder problems: the arms hang with the weights, a low-demand position; if holding the weights hurts, use bottles or a rucksack hugged at the thighs, or the unweighted hinge.

High blood pressure and heart disease: breathe out as you stand; do not hold the breath; use light weights and moderate effort; get medical clearance first if you have heart disease or uncontrolled blood pressure.

Osteoporosis: loaded strength work is generally recommended; avoid loaded spinal rounding and twisting; with severe osteoporosis or a prior vertebral fracture, ask a clinician first (reviews, snippets).

Pregnancy and postpartum: hinging is commonly kept with changes; coaches suggest a wider stance or a raised start to limit range; one ACSM-based guideline in a secondary source says keep RPE at 8/10 or below with some reps in reserve; ACOG's own wording was not reached, so ask your obstetrician, midwife or women's health physiotherapist; stop with pelvic heaviness, leaking or pain.
Mumbai flat: set the weights down gently, on a mat or towel, with a controlled lowering count; do not drop a dumbbell on a tile floor; no glass bottles; avoid the balcony slab.
